1.pericope_label: Children of the Lord: no cutting or baldness for the dead; a holy people; eat nothing abominable

schools.summary: Read the two verses as election, adoption and sanctification; take the cutting of the flesh to cover funeral grief, idolatrous self-wounding and the marking of the body for a deity; and turn the prohibition into a rule against immoderate sorrow.

Distinguish the special grace of adoption in some from the national adoption of all, and ground the obligation on the second; refer the cutting to Gentile custom in worship as well as mourning; and allow a thing to be abominable either in its nature or by prohibition.
Confine the cutting to the consecration of the hair to idols, making the incisions incidental; and reduce abomination to what God has forbidden.

Make sonship the foundation of every holiness law in the Pentateuch; trace the precept to its parallel in Leviticus and the second verse to its word-for-word source earlier in this book; correct the sense of the baldness; allow a sanitary purpose beside the ceremonial; and refer the exposition of the food laws away to Leviticus.

debates: What the cutting forbids: the consecration of the hair to a deity (Clarke) against incisions in the flesh at funerals and in idol worship (Henry, Gill).
Whether the food laws have any purpose beyond the ceremonial — Ellicott alone allows a sanitary one.
Whether a thing is abominable in its own nature or only by prohibition: Gill allows both, Wesley only the second.
Whether the sonship is national or personal — Gill separates the two, Henry treats the privileges as figures of what belongs to believers.
outliers: Clarke alone reads the prohibition of the hair rather than the flesh.
Henry alone supplies a rabbinic parallel, at second hand through an English editor, turning the law into a rule about grief.
Keil alone declines to expound the chapter at all, referring the reader to the parallel legislation.
Wesley’s two observations reproduce Henry’s in order and almost in wording, so the two are not independent witnesses.

4.pericope_label: The beasts that may be eaten, and the two marks of a clean beast

schools.summary: Set out how this list differs in function from the parallel in Leviticus — the permitted beasts specified here, the exceptions there; explain why the sacrificial animals stand first and what the generic terms allow for the passover victim; identify the disputed names against German and modern equivalents; infer from the range of species that the land was far less cleared than later; and, in Keil, refer the whole exposition away to Leviticus.

Classify each creature by Linnaean order, genus and species; ground the permission in physiology, the clean animals yielding the purest chyle from the best vegetable food; reject the received identification of the third beast in favour of the buffalo; and concede that two of the names are unrecoverable.
Derive the disputed name from a root of redness and canvass the Arabic for a swifter woodland animal; and reduce the whole question to the two marks, the parted hoof and the chewed cud.

debates: Whether this chapter needs exposition at all or should be referred to the parallel legislation: Keil sends it away, Clarke insists its particulars are new, Ellicott shows the two lists do different work.
What the third beast in the list is — a red deer or elk (Gill) against the buffalo (Clarke), with Ellicott attaching the buffalo to a different name entirely.
Whether the food law has a rationale in the wholesomeness of the flesh (Clarke) or is left as bare ceremonial prescription (the others).
Whether the last two names can be identified at all — Clarke declares them unrecoverable, Ellicott offers equivalents for both.
outliers: Clarke alone imports the Linnaean classification and the physiology of digestion into a commentary on the law.
Ellicott alone reasons from the species named to the state of cultivation in the land.
Keil alone supplies no exposition, his block reproducing the biblical text and breaking off inside it.

8.pericope_label: The swine; and the fish that have fins and scales

schools.summary: Read the rule of the waters as the counterpart of the rule of the beasts: two marks required together, the permission stated positively and the prohibition as its converse, with no exceptions and no degrees.

debates: Whether the two marks are required together or either alone suffices — Gill takes them as a pair, as with the parted hoof and the chewed cud.
outliers: Gill argues the rule from its parallel with the two marks of a clean beast rather than from the wording of the verse.

11.pericope_label: The clean birds may be eaten; the unclean birds named

schools.summary: Explain why only the unclean birds are listed, on the rabbinic ground that the clean kinds are more numerous; supply the Targum’s four marks of a clean bird; and treat the extra name as a possible scribal variant of one in the earlier list, two similar letters having been exchanged.
Count the list against the parallel and isolate the single difference, noting that three closely similar names stand where the earlier chapter has two.

Locate the trouble in the older translation rather than the text, the first name being wrongly rendered vulture in the earlier chapter while the third here is a distinct creature properly so rendered.

debates: Whether the extra name in this list is a distinct bird or a variant spelling of one already named: Ellicott and Clarke take it as a further creature, Gill weighs a scribal exchange of two similar letters.
Whether the earlier chapter’s rendering of the first name is correct — Clarke calls it improper and substitutes the kite or glede.
How a clean bird is to be recognised at all, the verse giving no marks: Gill supplies four from the Targum, the others let the list stand as exhaustive.
outliers: Gill alone gives positive marks for a clean bird, none being stated in the text.
Gill alone derives the sense of the disputed name from the bird’s eyesight rather than its flight.
Clarke alone corrects the older translation rather than the text.

19.pericope_label: Winged creeping things unclean; clean fowls; nothing that dies of itself; not seethe a kid in its mother’s milk

schools.summary: Give the Targum’s concrete instances of the unclean winged creatures and its permission of the locust; restrict the carcase to an animal dead of hunger or disease, impure from the manner of its death rather than in its kind; rest the law on the declared holiness of the people; separate it from the law of blood on the difference of penalty; and answer the objection that selling carrion to an alien supplies the materials of sin.

Read the clause about the stranger as describing what will happen rather than commanding it, state the purpose of the restrictions as raising Israel rather than degrading its neighbours, and place the prohibition of seething a kid as the last of three occurrences.
Report, without endorsing, the restriction of the milk prohibition to the paschal victim.

debates: Whether handing the carcase to a stranger licenses his sin: Calvin raises the objection and answers that the Gentiles lay under no distinction of meats; Ellicott answers instead from the purpose of the law and the freedom left to strangers.
Whether the flesh is unclean in itself or only from the manner of the animal’s death — Calvin insists on the second and argues from the order to throw it to dogs that a real contagion is meant.
Whether the clause about the stranger is command or description — Ellicott takes it as description of common practice.
What the prohibition of seething a kid forbids: a general rule, or only the offering of an unweaned paschal victim (reported by Clarke).
Whether the clean fowls of the permission are birds only — Gill admits the locust among them.
outliers: Calvin alone divides this law from the law of blood, and argues the division from the difference between the two penalties.
Calvin alone infers a real contagion in the meat from the direction to give it to dogs.
Ellicott alone denies that the law was framed to the disadvantage of other nations.
Gill alone specifies the unclean winged creatures, and does it from a Targum rather than from the text.

22.pericope_label: The second tithe: tithe all the increase, and eat it before the Lord in the place he chooses

schools.summary: Distinguish this tithe from the Levites’ portion and note that its measuring is left to the owner; argue that withholding or grudging it defrauds a brother of his maintenance; and deny that the whole land’s tithes can have gone to one place, reconstructing a local collection with a separate offering carried up.

Compute the two tithes as a fifth of the increase and call it an easy rent; make the owner’s self-assessment a deliberate trial of his fear of God; and draw the rule that what is laid by first is laid out more easily.
Set out the full six-year rotation of the second tithe between owners, Levites and the poor; and identify the second tithe with the third-year tithe.

Report the Jewish consensus that three passages describe one second tithe, distinct from the Levites’ and unlike it accounted holy; and meet the difficulty of distance by commutation to money at home, noting the different arrangement in the third and sixth years and the absence of a tithe in the sabbatical year.

debates: Whether the tithes of the whole land really went to the sanctuary: Calvin calls the plain sense absurd and reconstructs a local collection, while Keil and Ellicott accept it and solve the distance by allowing the tithe to be sold and the money carried.

How many tithes there were and how they rotated — Clarke’s six-year cycle, Ellicott’s Talmudic identification of three passages as one, and Wesley’s identification of the second tithe with the third-year tithe.
Whether the first tithe was sacred: Ellicott reports that it was not and that the second always was.
Whether leaving the measurement to the owner is a concession or a test — Henry alone makes it a deliberate trial of the fear of God.
outliers: Calvin alone declares the command, as commonly read, absurd, and rejects the standing conjecture of earlier commentators as an improbable doubling of the burden.
Calvin alone argues from the futility of carrying grain up and back, and from the threats against defrauding priests, that the Levites must have collected locally.
Henry alone reckons the total charge on the increase and judges it light.
Ellicott alone follows the rule into the sabbatical year and concludes there was no tithe to pay.

24.pericope_label: If the way is too long, turn the tithe into money; buy and eat before the Lord; forsake not the Levite

schools.summary: Deny that this concession concerns the tithe, on the ground that the redemption ordinance requires an added fifth which is missing here and that the sequel speaks of offerings; read the liberty of purchase at its widest; and hold that the Levite must be taken along to the meal, not merely remembered.

Take the clause as the tithe’s commutation and expound the Hebrew of binding the silver; report the strict Jewish limits on what the second tithe might buy and the Talmudic treatise devoted to them; infer from the mention of strong drink that its use is not sinful; and state the third-year rule, which keeps the tithe in the towns rather than sending it to the sanctuary.
Identify the strong drink from the parallel legislation and take the verse as evidence that the law made ample provision for the comfort and happiness of the people.

debates: Whether the commutation clause concerns the tithe at all: Calvin denies it from the missing fifth of the redemption law and from the language of offerings that follows, while Keil and Gill take it straightforwardly as the tithe turned into money.
How wide the liberty of purchase is — Gill allows whatever suits the appetite, Ellicott reports a rabbinic tradition permitting only what the verse names.
What the mention of strong drink establishes: that its use is not sinful in itself (Ellicott) or that the law provided generously for human comfort (Clarke).
outliers: Calvin alone detaches the passage from the law of tithes and reads it of offerings generally.
Ellicott alone cites the Talmudic treatise governing the second tithe.
Keil alone carries the exposition forward into the third-year rule and notes that the tithe then stays in the towns.

28.pericope_label: The third-year tithe laid up in the gates for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow

schools.summary: Weigh the case for a distinct third tithe and reject it, reading the passage as a correction of the law lest the clergy consume the whole; count the third year from the sabbatical so the rule never falls on a fallow year; and explain the diversion as withdrawing part of the Levites’ abundance lest it breed luxury.

Identify the impost as the poor’s tithe of Jewish usage; deny the rabbinic division that gives the Levite the first tithe and the poor the second; and turn a rabbinic reading against the critics who find the tithe laws of Deuteronomy and Numbers contradictory, distinguishing an ordinary rate for the ministry from a tithe taken for God.

Fix the sense of “at the end of three years” as the third and not the fourth year from the parallel passage; and explain the Levite’s dependence on freewill offerings as designed to bind minister and people to each other.

debates: Whether a third tithe is meant or the second redirected: an older Jewish authority and one text of a deuterocanonical book support a third, while the general Jewish view, Ellicott and Calvin make it the second turned to the poor.
Why the ministry is left dependent: Clarke reads the arrangement as an incentive to faithful labour and grateful support, Calvin as a check on clerical abundance and luxury.
Whether the Levite here receives the first tithe or shares the poor’s: the rabbinic view is reported by Gill and partly followed, and flatly rejected by Ellicott.
Whether “at the end of three years” means the third year or the fourth — raised and settled by Wesley alone.
Whether the tithe law of this book contradicts the earlier legislation — Ellicott argues from ancient Jewish practice that it does not.
outliers: Calvin alone shows that the third year must be counted from the sabbatical, or the rule would fall on a fallow year.
Calvin alone computes what the arrangement leaves the Levites and treats the reduction as a safeguard against luxury.
Clarke alone gives a positive rationale for clerical dependence on freewill offerings.
Ellicott alone uses a rabbinic opinion he rejects as evidence against a critical theory of the law’s composition.
